learn.b: Every program is a list of instructions. The print function shows a value in the Output window, which is how you check what your code is doing. Text goes inside quotes, numbers do not.
learn.code:
print("Hello, world!")
print(42)

learn.b: A variable is a name that holds a value. You write the name, an equals sign, then the value. Later you can use the name instead of the value, or give it a new value.
learn.code:
score = 10
print(score)
score = 15
print(score)

learn.b: Writing local before the name keeps the variable inside the script or block where you made it. It is faster and stops different scripts from mixing up their variables. Good Luau code uses local almost every time.
learn.code:
local coins = 5
local playerName = "Rob"
print(playerName, coins)

learn.b: Two dashes start a comment, which Luau ignores. Names are case sensitive, cannot start with a number, and are usually written in camelCase. A variable with no value holds nil, which means nothing.
learn.code:
-- this is a comment
local Coins = 1
local coins = 2
local empty
print(empty)

learn.b: Luau does math with + - * / and the percent sign gives the remainder after dividing. The caret ^ raises to a power. Math follows the usual order: powers first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
learn.code:
print(7 + 3 * 2)
print(10 % 3)
print(2 ^ 3)

learn.b: A string is text inside quotes. You can use double or single quotes, just match the pair. Putting a hash sign before a string gives its length.
learn.code:
local name = "Roblox"
print(#name)
print('single quotes work too')

learn.b: Two dots join strings together, which is called concatenation. Numbers are turned into text when you join them. Remember to add spaces inside the quotes yourself.
learn.code:
local n = 7
print("Level " .. n)
print("Hi " .. "Sam" .. "!")

learn.b: tostring turns a value into a string, and tonumber turns text that looks like a number into a number. If the text is not a number, tonumber gives nil. Use these when you read numbers from text.
learn.code:
local t = "25"
print(tonumber(t) + 5)
print(tostring(99) .. " points")

learn.b: An if statement runs code only when its condition is true. You write if, the condition, then, the code, and finish with end. Without end Luau does not know where the block stops.
learn.code:
local hp = 0
if hp <= 0 then
    print("You died")
end

learn.b: To compare, use == for equal, ~= for not equal, and < > <= >= for size. A single = is for giving a value to a variable, not for comparing. Every comparison gives true or false.
learn.code:
print(5 == 5)
print(5 ~= 5)
print(3 >= 4)

learn.b: and needs both sides to be true, or needs at least one, and not flips true and false. You can build bigger conditions from them. Use brackets when it gets confusing.
learn.code:
local age = 14
if age >= 13 and age < 20 then
    print("teenager")
end

learn.b: Add elseif to test another condition when the first one fails. Add else at the end for everything left over. Luau checks from the top and runs only the first block that is true.
learn.code:
local x = 15
if x > 20 then
    print("big")
elseif x > 10 then
    print("medium")
else
    print("small")
end

qs.q: Which operator means not equal in Luau?
qs.why: Luau writes not equal as ~=.

qs.q: Which keyword closes an if block?
qs.why: Every if block finishes with end.

qs.q: What does this print?
qs.code:
local x = 15

    print("big")
elseif x > 10 then
    print("medium")
else
    print("small")
end
qs.why: 15 is not above 20 but it is above 10, so the elseif runs.

qs.q: To check if two values are equal in an if, you write a single = sign.
qs.why: Comparing uses ==. A single = gives a value to a variable.

lab.q: Challenge: n is a whole number. Print even if it is even, otherwise print odd.
lab.hint: A number is even when n % 2 == 0.
lab.solution:

    print('even')
else

lab.why: The remainder after dividing by 2 tells you if a number is even.

lab.q: Challenge: score is set. Print A if it is 90 or more, B if it is 70 or more, otherwise C.
lab.hint: Check the highest score first with if, then elseif, then else.

    print('A')
elseif score >= 70 then
    print('B')
else

end
lab.why: The chain stops at the first true condition.

learn.b: for i = 1, 5 do runs the code with i counting from 1 to 5, including 5. You can add a third number as the step, and a negative step counts down. Use it when you know how many times to repeat.
learn.code:
for i = 1, 3 do
    print(i)
end
for i = 10, 1, -4 do
    print(i)
end

learn.b: A while loop checks its condition before every run and repeats while it is true. Make sure something inside the loop changes the condition, or it never ends. A loop that never ends will freeze your game.
learn.code:
local n = 3
while n > 0 do
    print(n)
    n = n - 1
end

learn.b: A repeat loop runs the body first and checks the condition at the end. That means it always runs at least once. It stops when the condition after until becomes true.
learn.code:
local tries = 0
repeat
    tries = tries + 1
until tries >= 3
print(tries)

learn.b: The break keyword leaves the loop right away. It is useful when you found what you were looking for and do not need to keep going. It works in while, repeat and for loops.
learn.code:
for i = 1, 100 do
    if i * i > 50 then
        print(i)
        break
    end
end

qs.why: The loop counts 1, 2 and 3, and includes the last number.

qs.why: repeat checks the condition after the body.

qs.why: It starts at 10 and subtracts 4 each time: 10, 6, 2. The next, -2, is below 1.

qs.why: until works as the stop condition.

lab.q: Challenge: n is set. Use a loop to print the sum of the numbers from 1 to n.
lab.hint: Keep a total and add i in a for loop.
lab.solution:

    total = total + i
end
print(total)

lab.q: Challenge: n is set. Use a while loop to print n down to 1 on separate lines, then print Go!
lab.hint: while n > 0 do ... n = n - 1 end
lab.solution:

    print(n)
    n = n - 1
end

learn.b: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again. You write function, a name, brackets with inputs, the code, and end. Nothing happens until you call the function by its name with brackets.
learn.code:
local function greet(name)
    print("Hi " .. name)
end
greet("Sam")
greet("Mia")

learn.b: The return keyword sends a value back to the code that called the function. Code after return in the same block does not run. A function with no return gives back nil.
learn.code:
local function add(a, b)
    return a + b
end
local result = add(2, 3)
print(result)

learn.b: The names in the brackets of the definition are parameters. The real values you pass when calling are arguments. They are copied into the parameters in order.
learn.code:
local function area(w, h)
    return w * h
end
print(area(3, 4))

learn.b: A function can return several values separated by commas. Functions are values, so you can store them in variables and pass them to other functions. Variables made with local inside a function disappear when it ends.
learn.code:
local function minMax(a, b)
    if a < b then return a, b end
    return b, a
end
local low, high = minMax(9, 4)
print(low, high)

qs.why: return hands a value back to the caller.

qs.why: Without return, the result is nil.

lab.q: Challenge: write a function named bigger(a, b) that returns the larger number.
lab.starter:
local function bigger(a, b)
    -- your code
end
lab.hint: Use if a > b then return a end, then return b.
lab.solution:

lab.q: Challenge: write a function named isEven(n) that returns true if n is even, otherwise false.

    -- your code
end
lab.hint: A comparison like n % 2 == 0 already gives true or false.
lab.solution:

lab.why: A comparison can be returned directly.

learn.b: A table is Luau's one container type. With values in curly brackets separated by commas it works as an array, a numbered list. Counting starts at 1, not 0, and you read items with square brackets.
A hash sign before the table gives how many items it has. table.insert adds an item to the end, and table.remove takes one out by position. The last item is always at position #t.
learn.code:
local t = {5, 10}
table.insert(t, 15)
print(#t)
print(t[#t])
table.remove(t, 1)
print(t[1])

learn.b: for i, v in ipairs(t) goes through the array in order. i is the position and v is the value. Use an underscore name like _ when you do not need the position.
learn.code:
local t = {4, 8, 15}
for i, v in ipairs(t) do
    print(i, v)
end

learn.b: You can change an item by assigning to its position. table.concat joins the items of an array into one string with a separator you choose. Items can be numbers, strings, or even other tables.

learn.b: A table can also store values under names, called keys. You write key = value pairs in the curly brackets. Read a value with a dot and the key, like player.coins.
Assign to a key to change it, or to make a new one. Setting a key to nil deletes it. You can also use square brackets with a string, which helps when the key is in a variable.
learn.code:
local p = {hp = 10}
p.hp = p.hp + 5
p.mana = 3
p.mana = nil
local k = "hp"
print(p[k])

learn.b: for key, value in pairs(t) goes through every pair in a dictionary. The order is not guaranteed, so do not rely on it. Use pairs for dictionaries and ipairs for numbered arrays.
learn.code:
local stock = {apples = 3, pears = 5}
local total = 0
for name, n in pairs(stock) do
    total = total + n
end
print(total)

learn.b: A missing key gives nil, so you can test if t.key ~= nil then. Tables can hold other tables, which lets you build things like a list of players. Chain the dots to dig in.

learn.b: Strings have built-in methods you call with a colon. upper and lower change the case, rep repeats the text, and len gives the length. The original string never changes, you get a new one back.
learn.code:
local s = "Roblox"
print(s:upper())
print(s:lower())
print(("ab"):rep(3))
print(s:len())

learn.b: s:sub(i, j) gives the part from position i to position j, counting from 1 and including both ends. With one number it goes to the end. A negative number counts from the back.
learn.code:
local s = "Roblox"
print(s:sub(1, 3))
print(s:sub(4))
print(s:sub(-2))

learn.b: s:find(text) gives the start and end position of the first match, or nil if there is none. s:gsub(a, b) replaces every a with b and also returns how many it replaced. Wrap it in brackets to keep only the new string.
learn.code:
local s = "banana"
print(s:find("nan"))
print((s:gsub("a", "o")))

learn.b: string.format builds text from a template. %s is a slot for a string, and %d is a slot for a whole number. It is cleaner than joining many pieces with two dots.
learn.code:
local name, score = "Ann", 7
print(string.format("%s scored %d", name, score))

learn.b: In Roblox Studio, every object such as a Part, a Sound or a Folder is an Instance. Instance.new creates one from its class name. The new object is invisible to the game until you give it a parent.
learn.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
print(part.ClassName)

learn.b: Properties describe an object, like Size, Position, Color and Anchored. You set them with a dot. Sizes and positions use Vector3.new(x, y, z), and colors use Color3.fromRGB or BrickColor.
learn.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 4)
part.Position = Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)
part.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 0, 0)
part.Anchored = true

learn.b: The Parent property decides where an object lives. Setting Parent to workspace puts a Part into the 3D world so players can see it. It is best practice to set Parent last, after the other properties.
learn.code:
local part = Instance.new("Part")
part.Anchored = true
part.Parent = workspace
print(part.Parent.Name)

learn.b: FindFirstChild looks inside an object for a child with a given name and gives nil if it is missing. Destroy removes an object for good. A script can reach its own parent with script.Parent.
learn.code:
local door = workspace:FindFirstChild("Door")
if door then
    door:Destroy()
end

learn.b: An event is a signal Roblox sends when something happens, like a part being touched or a player joining. You do not check over and over. You tell Roblox which function to run when the event fires.
learn.code:
local part = script.Parent
print(part.Name)

learn.b: Every event has a Connect method that takes a function. That function runs each time the event fires, and it can keep running many times. Touched fires when something touches a Part, and passes the part that touched it.
learn.code:
local part = script.Parent
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    print(hit.Name)
end)

learn.b: When a character touches a part, hit is one of its body parts, such as a Leg. Its Parent is the character, and the character holds a Humanoid. Checking for the Humanoid tells you a character touched it, not just a block.
learn.code:
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    local humanoid = hit.Parent:FindFirstChild("Humanoid")
    if humanoid then
        humanoid.Health = 0
    end
end)

learn.b: game:GetService("Players") gives the Players service. Its PlayerAdded event fires for every player who joins and passes that player. Connect returns a connection, and calling Disconnect on it stops listening.
learn.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    print("Welcome " .. player.Name)
end)

learn.b: A Roblox game runs on a server, which all players share, and on each player's own device, called the client. A Script runs on the server, and a LocalScript runs on one player's client. The server is the boss: it decides what is real.
learn.code:
-- Script (server): in ServerScriptService
print("I run on the server")
-- LocalScript (client): in StarterPlayerScripts
print("I run on one player")

learn.b: If a client changes something, such as a Part, only that player sees it. Things like coins, damage and items must be changed by the server so everyone agrees. A cheater can edit anything on their own client, so never trust it.
A RemoteEvent is a message pipe between client and server. Put it in ReplicatedStorage so both sides can see it. The client calls FireServer to send, and the server listens with OnServerEvent.
learn.code:
-- Client
remote:FireServer("Sword")
-- Server
remote.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, item)
    print(item)
end)

learn.b: The server always receives the player who fired as the first argument, so you never pass it yourself. To talk the other way, the server calls FireClient for one player or FireAllClients for everyone. The client listens with OnClientEvent.
learn.code:
-- Server
remote:FireClient(player, "You won!")
-- Client
remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(message)
    print(message)
end)

learn.b: A ModuleScript lets you keep code in one place and use it from many scripts. It must end with return, usually a table of functions. Other scripts load it with require.
learn.code:
-- ModuleScript named Util
local Util = {}
function Util.double(n)
    return n * 2
end
return Util

-- another script
local Util = require(script.Parent.Util)
print(Util.double(4))

learn.b: Luau is Lua with optional types. You write a colon and a type after a variable or parameter, like number, string or boolean. Types catch mistakes while you type, and putting --!strict at the top of a script checks them strictly.
learn.code:
--!strict
local name: string = "Sam"
local function add(a: number, b: number): number
    return a + b
end
print(add(2, 3))

learn.b: task.wait(seconds) pauses the script for that long and then continues. It replaces the old wait function and is more accurate. Use it in loops so they do not freeze the game.
learn.code:
for i = 3, 1, -1 do
    print(i)
    task.wait(1)
end
print("Go!")

learn.b: task.spawn runs a function right now on its own, so the main script keeps going without waiting. task.delay runs a function after some seconds. Luau also has +=, so score += 1 means score = score + 1.
learn.code:
task.spawn(function()
    task.wait(2)
    print("B")
end)
print("A")
task.delay(1, function()
    print("later")
end)

qs.why: task.wait takes the number of seconds.

    return n * 2
end
return Util

-- Another script

print(U.double(4))
qs.why: double(4) returns 4 * 2.
